newsitem.title: DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF CONGO: Hints of massacre probe progress in Kabila's Congo.
newsitem.headline: Hints of massacre probe progress in Kabila's Congo.

text.p: Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of the Congo and the United Nations on Friday tried to break a deadlock over terms of an investigation into alleged massacres of Hutu refugees, with a hint of progress in the air.
A member of a U.N. advance team told Reuters ahead of a meeting with the government later on Friday that despite the obstacles, progress could not be ruled out.
"We are close to reaching an agreement on the principles of an investigation," John Mills said, but added: "This does not mean that we have solved the two non-negotiable issues."
Kabila's government refuses to accept Chilean lawyer Roberto Garreton, U.N. rapporteur or special investiagtor for the area since 1994, as a member of the mission.

It also wants the team to extend the inquiry beyond its seven-month civil war that toppled the former Zaire's veteran dictator Mobutu Sese Seko to include the aftermath of the 1994 genocide in Rwanda of minority Tutsis by Hutu hardliners.

Kabila's National Reconstruction and Emergency Planning Minister Etienne Richard Mbaya told a Kinshasa news conference on Thursday that the investigation could begin on time on July 7 only if the U.N. accepted minimum conditions.
"Our sovereignty is important to us," he said.
U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan told reporters in Geneva on Thursday the goal was to get at the facts of what happened and he was prepared to be flexible if that was what was needed.
"The most important thing is for us to get to the facts," he said. "The alleged mass killings ought to be investigated."

The investigation follows allegations that Kabila's Tutsi-backed rebels or their Rwandan or Ugandan allies killed Rwandan Hutu refugees as their forces marched across former Zaire between October and May and toppled Mobutu.

In April, Garreton accused Kabila's rebels of massacring Hutu refugees during their push across Africa's third largest nation. "Garreton produced a report full of lies," Mbaya said. "The U.N. has other personalities."
Mbaya said Hutu hardliners responsible for the Rwanda genocide had forcibly stopped fellow Hutus from returning home.
Kabila's Foreign Minister Bizima Karaha told Reuters Television the investigators were free to go where they wanted.

"We are the ones who asked for the U.N investigators to come," Karaha told Reuters Africa Journal, saying the only mass graves were for cholera victims or people killed by hardliners who held fellow Rwandan Hutus hostage in the then Zaire.
"We really want to help these people to do a good job, not for us but for the so-called refugees. There is no resistance, we told them they are free to go anywhere."

The advance team, including Argentine forensic experts who would excavate sites suspected to contain mass graves in former Zaire, has been in Kinshasa for two weeks seeking accord on the terms for the full investigation due to start on Monday.
Annan said the U.N. would like Garreton to stay in charge, but added: "If that doesn't happen we are not going to let them (Kinshasa) use that to prevent us from getting to the facts."

Most of the Hutu refugees flooded out of Rwanda in 1994 fearing reprisals after armed Tutsis exiles returned and drove out the Hutu hardliners responsible for the genocide. Others fled from the Tutsi-dominated army in neighbouring Burundi.
